title: The Galaxy's Fastest Star Could Reveal the Secrets of a Supermassive Black Hole
gist: Astronomers have identified S301, the fastest-known star in the Milky Way, on a tight 8.7-year orbit around the supermassive black hole Sagittarius A*, and believe tracking its path over the next decade could let them measure the black hole's spin for the first time.

insights.claim: Astronomers have detected S301, the fastest-known star in the Milky Way, reaching a top speed of 25,000 kilometers per second (about 8 percent of the speed of light) as it orbits Sagittarius A*, the supermassive black hole at the galaxy's center, completing one orbit every 8.7 years.
insights.speaker: Jorge Garay
insights.so_what: Establishes a new record-setting object useful as an extreme physics laboratory close to a supermassive black hole.
insights.locator: S301, as astronomers have named the star, reaches 25,000 kilometers per second

insights.claim: At its closest approach to Sagittarius A*, S301 comes within a distance comparable to the gap between Saturn and the sun, and its speed varies sharply across its highly elongated orbit, moving fastest near the black hole and slower farther away, similar to how comets like Halley's Comet behave in the solar system.
insights.speaker: Jorge Garay
insights.so_what: Quantifies just how close S301 gets to a supermassive black hole, which is what makes it uniquely useful for testing gravitational effects.
insights.locator: According to the European Southern Observatory (ESO), at its closest approach

insights.claim: The European Southern Observatory concludes that S301 was likely originally part of a binary star pair torn apart by Sagittarius A*'s tidal forces, with S301 captured into its current tight orbit while its companion star was likely ejected with enough velocity to leave the galaxy entirely.
insights.speaker: Jorge Garay
insights.so_what: Offers a mechanistic explanation (the Hills mechanism) for how stars end up in extreme orbits this close to a black hole, since stars cannot form there directly.
insights.quote: S301's orbital properties, and the fact that stars cannot form so close to a massive black hole, indicate that the star was likely part of a binary pair that was torn apart by the tidal forces of Sagittarius A*.

themes.theme: Scientific payoff: measuring black hole spin

insights.claim: Astronomers believe that within about 10 years, by tracking small deviations in S301's orbit caused by frame-dragging (the warping of spacetime predicted by general relativity for a rotating mass), they will be able to determine the spin of Sagittarius A* — something that would otherwise require several more decades of observation using other known stars like S2.
insights.speaker: Jorge Garay
insights.so_what: S301 could dramatically accelerate a long-standing open problem in black hole astrophysics — measuring spin — turning a decades-long observation program into a roughly 10-year one.
insights.locator: Astronomers believe that within 10 years they will be able to determine the rotation of Sagittarius A*

insights.claim: S301 was first detected in 2023 using the GRAVITY instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope Interferometer (VLTI) in Chile, and researchers traced its movement backward through archival observations dating to 2017 to reconstruct its orbit, determining it made its closest approach to Sagittarius A* in early 2023 and will do so again in 2031.
insights.speaker: Jorge Garay
insights.so_what: Sets a concrete near-term observational milestone (2031 close approach) for follow-up measurements of the black hole's spin.
insights.locator: Astronomers first detected S301 in 2023 using GRAVITY
